variants.title: Run the evidence path
variants.context: The caption path keeps generation and release apart: normalize the image and task, build a visual representation, decode bounded candidates, ground each parsed claim against evidence, then let policy decide what may be released. The decoder proposes language and the release layer holds the authority.
variants.prompt: A catalog image with a small printed size label enters the captioning service. Put the stages in order.

items.text: Decode one or more bounded candidate captions under the declared length limit.
Normalize the image at a resolution that still preserves the smallest supported text region.
Retain the supported claims, remove unsafe detail, and log the complete verdict with model and evidence versions.
Parse objects, attributes, actions, relations, and quoted text, then link each claim to a region, verified OCR, or trusted context.
Build patch, region, and global features, and store the OCR text with its coordinates and verification status.

variants.hint: One early choice decides whether the small label can be grounded at all.
variants.explanation: Resolution and region identity are chosen before generation, because a claim can only be linked to evidence the representation kept.

variants.title: Run the evidence path
variants.context: The caption path keeps generation and release apart: normalize the image and task, build a visual representation, decode bounded candidates, ground each parsed claim against evidence, then let policy decide what may be released. variants.prompt: A candidate caption names a brand that no region, OCR span, or approved record supports. Put the stages in order.

items.text: Decode a fluent candidate in which the brand name receives high decoder confidence.
Normalize the image under the declared use case and locale.
Release the caption with the unsupported claim removed and the removal recorded.
Encode the image into region and global features for the grounding step to reference.
Fail to link the brand claim to any region, verified OCR span, or trusted metadata.

variants.hint: High decoder confidence is a preference signal, not evidence.
variants.explanation: The release layer removes the unsupported claim and logs the removal, so a likely token never becomes a released fact.

variants.prompt: A medical scan reaches a general captioning route. Put the stages in order, ending with the correct outcome.

items.text: Encode the image while the policy boundary flags the regulated domain.
Escalate to the approved reviewer instead of returning the generated sentence.
Normalize the image and read the declared use case from the request contract.
Detect a forbidden inference during claim grounding and policy evaluation.
Decode a bounded candidate that includes a diagnostic sounding phrase.

variants.hint: Forbidden claims are blocked no matter how well they score.
variants.explanation: Policy boundaries forbid unsupported identity, diagnosis, and other sensitive inferences independently of any similarity or consensus score.

variants.title: Degrade without bypassing trust
variants.context: Degrading a captioning service must never bypass its trust checks. The ladder runs from reducing candidates and length, to a batch tier with durable job state, to a conservative partial caption, to the approved reviewer, and finally to an explicit no caption result.
variants.prompt: Load rises across every captioning route at once. Put the degradation steps in order from cheapest to most restrictive.

items.text: Move eligible catalog work to a batch tier with durable job state.
Return an explicit no caption result when grounding or policy dependencies are unavailable.
Return a conservative partial caption when the supported facts are still useful.
Route regulated or ambiguous cases to the approved reviewer.
Reduce candidate count and maximum length while keeping evidence and safety checks in place.

variants.hint: Every step keeps the checks; only the ambition of the output falls.
variants.explanation: Degradation reduces how much the system promises, never how much it verifies.

variants.title: Degrade without bypassing trust
variants.context: Degrading a captioning service must never bypass its trust checks. The ladder runs from reducing candidates and length, to a batch tier with durable job state, to a conservative partial caption, to the approved reviewer, and finally to an explicit no caption result.
variants.prompt: A traffic spike hits the catalog route while the accessibility route must stay interactive. Put the steps in order.

items.text: Send the cases that fall below the evidence threshold to the reviewer queue.
Cut the candidate count and maximum length on the interactive route first.
Serve conservative partial captions for the remaining interactive requests.
Push the catalog re captioning backlog to the batch tier so it cannot consume the interactive deadline.

variants.hint: Background work should be the first thing to move.
variants.explanation: Separating batch work from interactive traffic protects the deadline before output quality has to be reduced.

variants.title: Degrade without bypassing trust
variants.context: Degrading a captioning service must never bypass its trust checks. The ladder runs from reducing candidates and length, to a batch tier with durable job state, to a conservative partial caption, to the approved reviewer, and finally to an explicit no caption result.
variants.prompt: The grounding service goes down during a release. Put the steps in order, ending with the correct terminal outcome.

items.text: Discover that new requests cannot obtain any claim evidence at all.
Try the conservative partial caption path for requests whose claims were already grounded.
Shrink candidate generation to conserve the remaining capacity.
Return an explicit no caption result rather than releasing ungrounded text.

variants.hint: There is a terminal outcome that is not a caption.
variants.explanation: No caption is a valid product outcome; releasing fluent prose without its grounding dependency is not.

variants.title: Compute required fact coverage
variants.context: Coverage is required facts included divided by required facts for the task, pooled across the cases in the slice being measured. It is reported next to hallucination and safety results, never averaged into them.
variants.prompt: A frozen evaluation set declares 40 required facts across its cases. The candidate run includes 34 of them. What is the coverage?
variants.hint: Coverage counts what was included, not what was missed.
variants.explanation: Coverage is 34 divided by 40, which is 85 percent, and it is compared against the route's declared coverage floor.

mistakes.feedback: Reported the omission rate instead of the coverage rate.
Gave the count of missing facts rather than a percentage.

variants.title: Compute required fact coverage
variants.context: Coverage is required facts included divided by required facts for the task, pooled across the cases in the slice being measured. It is reported next to hallucination and safety results, never averaged into them.
variants.prompt: The low light slice has three cases requiring 4, 3, and 5 facts. The run covers 3, 2, and 4 of them. What is the coverage for this slice?
variants.explanation: The slice covers 9 of 12 required facts, which is 75 percent; pooling by fact keeps a small case from carrying the same weight as a large one.

mistakes.feedback: Reported the share of facts omitted instead of covered.
Averaged the three per case rates instead of pooling the facts.

variants.title: Compute required fact coverage
variants.context: Coverage is required facts included divided by required facts for the task, pooled across the cases in the slice being measured. It is reported next to hallucination and safety results, never averaged into them.
variants.prompt: The accessibility slice has two cases requiring 4 and 6 facts, and the run covers 8 of them in total. Overall coverage across all slices is 85 percent. What is the coverage for the accessibility slice?
variants.hint: The slice has its own denominator.
variants.explanation: The slice covers 8 of 10 required facts, or 80 percent, and a slice floor is checked separately from the overall number.

mistakes.feedback: Reported the omitted share instead of the covered share.
Reused the overall coverage instead of computing the slice.

variants.title: Pick the right control
variants.context: Decoding controls and grounding thresholds do different jobs. Beam width and sampling change which candidates exist, lexical constraints force wording, and evidence thresholds act on parsed claims after generation and must be calibrated per evidence source and use case.
variants.prompt: A reranker can only ever choose from one candidate, and the team wants it to compare real alternatives. What should change?
options: Raise the length penalty so the single caption carries more detail.
Widen the beam so more complete candidates reach the reranker.
Lower the evidence threshold so more claims survive grounding.
optionFeedback: A longer caption is still one candidate, and extra detail adds hallucination risk.
Correct: beam width controls how many complete candidates exist for a reranker to compare.
That releases weaker claims instead of producing anything new to choose between.
variants.hint: Which knob changes how many candidates exist?
variants.explanation: Greedy decoding never compares complete alternatives, so a wider beam is what gives the reranker something to select from; it also costs more decoder work.

variants.title: Pick the right control
variants.context: Decoding controls and grounding thresholds do different jobs. Beam width and sampling change which candidates exist, lexical constraints force wording, and evidence thresholds act on parsed claims after generation and must be calibrated per evidence source and use case.
variants.prompt: Verified OCR claims and detector claims are both released at the same 0.8 evidence threshold, and OCR errors are reaching users. What is the right fix?
options: Treat the threshold as a probability that the claim is true.
Drop OCR claims entirely and describe only the visible objects.
Calibrate the evidence threshold separately for each evidence source.
optionFeedback: A threshold is a calibrated decision boundary, not a probability of truth.
Removing readable text throws away the evidence that many routes exist to deliver.
Correct: thresholds are per source and per use case, not one universal number.
variants.hint: Do two different evidence sources produce comparable confidence values?
variants.explanation: Grounding thresholds act after generation and must be calibrated per evidence source and use case, because one source's 0.8 is not another's.

variants.title: Pick the right control
variants.context: Decoding controls and grounding thresholds do different jobs. Beam width and sampling change which candidates exist, lexical constraints force wording, and evidence thresholds act on parsed claims after generation and must be calibrated per evidence source and use case.
variants.prompt: A catalog route must always state the product size, and the team adds a lexical constraint that forces the phrase into every caption. What is the risk?
options: The constraint will make the caption fail image text compatibility scoring.
The constraint can force a size claim that no evidence supports.
The constraint will slow decoding beyond the route's latency budget.
optionFeedback: Compatibility scoring is a diagnostic here and is not the failure that reaches the user.
Correct: a required phrase is wording, and wording alone cannot establish that the fact is visible.
Constraint decoding costs some work, but latency is not what makes this unsafe.
variants.hint: What does a constraint guarantee, the words or the fact?
variants.explanation: Lexical constraints are useful for terminology and structure, but the release layer must still drop a required field when no evidence supports it.

variants.title: Match the evidence to its question
variants.context: No single number represents caption quality. Consensus wording, semantic propositions, image text compatibility, and claim failures each answer a different question, and the hard release gates stay conjunctive so one strong axis cannot pay for a failure on another.
variants.prompt: Match each evaluation signal to the question it actually answers.

pairs.label: CIDEr
pairs.detail: How closely does the wording match weighted human consensus across several references?

pairs.label: SPICE
pairs.detail: Do the objects, attributes, and relations in the scene graph agree with the references?

pairs.label: CLIPScore
pairs.detail: How compatible is the caption with the image representation, with no reference needed?

pairs.label: CHAIR
pairs.detail: How often does the caption mention objects that the ground truth says are absent?

variants.hint: Two of these need references, one does not, and one counts a specific failure.
variants.explanation: A portfolio is needed because a reference set cannot enumerate every valid caption and a similarity score cannot enumerate every unsupported claim.

variants.title: Match the evidence to its question
variants.context: No single number represents caption quality. Consensus wording, semantic propositions, image text compatibility, and claim failures each answer a different question, and the hard release gates stay conjunctive so one strong axis cannot pay for a failure on another.
variants.prompt: Match each hard release gate to the failure it blocks.

pairs.label: Hallucination gate
pairs.detail: Unsupported claims exceed the declared case or claim limit.

pairs.label: Coverage gate
pairs.detail: Too much task required information is missing, even when every released claim is true.

pairs.label: Safety gate
pairs.detail: A forbidden sensitive inference appears, whatever the similarity scores say.

pairs.label: Slice gate
pairs.detail: A required slice falls below its floor or diverges too far from the best slice.

pairs.label: Operational gate
pairs.detail: Latency, availability, review capacity, or cost per released caption is out of contract.

variants.hint: One gate fires when the captions are true but too thin.
variants.explanation: The gates stay conjunctive so a strong average cannot pay for a specific failure that reaches a specific user.

variants.title: Match the evidence to its question
variants.context: No single number represents caption quality. Consensus wording, semantic propositions, image text compatibility, and claim failures each answer a different question, and the hard release gates stay conjunctive so one strong axis cannot pay for a failure on another.
variants.prompt: Match each observed symptom to the measurement that exposes it.

pairs.label: Captions read well and score well, yet name objects that are not there
pairs.detail: Claim level hallucination counts, not sentence overlap scores.

pairs.label: Every released claim is true, but users still miss what they needed
pairs.detail: Required fact coverage for the declared task.

pairs.label: The overall numbers are healthy while night photos fail
pairs.detail: Slice reporting by lighting, language, and image type.

pairs.label: Scores improved because the hard cases stopped being answered
pairs.detail: Abstention and review volume reported next to quality.

variants.hint: Two of these look like success until you change what you count.
variants.explanation: Hiding difficult cases can raise released caption scores, so abstention and review volume are reported alongside quality rather than after it.
